reframing_when: The question asks 'should we do X?' without naming what is given up by doing X — the hidden cost of saying yes is invisible.
The question pursues one objective as though it has no tension with other objectives — competing demands are unacknowledged.
The question treats resource allocation as unbounded ('we should do everything') when time, money, or attention are scarce and force explicit prioritization.
The question optimizes for a single metric without asking what other metrics degrade when that one improves — the compression-vs-comprehensiveness tension is unexamined.
reframing_move: Surface the hidden cost: instead of 'should we do X?', ask 'what are we giving up by doing X, and is that sacrifice worth making?' — forces the question to acknowledge that every yes is a no to something else.
curation_note: Trade-offs is a primary reframing tool because its core function is making invisible costs visible at the question level. The source is explicit: 'if one cannot think in terms of trade-offs, they are a danger to the rest of the people when serious thinking is being done.' The model converts single-objective questions into multi-objective ones.

reframing_when.note: All four activations derived from source: hidden cost of yes (Kelleher example), competing objectives (balancing act analogy), resource scarcity forcing prioritization (don't boil the ocean), and single-metric optimization (compression vs comprehensiveness).

frame_patterns_challenged.note: Proxy optimization: the question optimizes for a proxy without surfacing what degrades. Option space collapse: surfacing trade-offs reveals hidden alternatives. Borrowed premise: inherited framing hides the cost of the chosen path.
